reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: Most commonly fractured carpal bone, typically following a fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist dorsiflexed and radially deviated
Hallmark signs are tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, tenderness over the scaphoid tubercle, and pain on axial compression of the thumb
The scaphoid receives its blood supply retrogradely through vessels entering distally, so waist and proximal pole fractures place the proximal fragment at risk of avascular necrosis and non-union
Initial radiographs are frequently normal (occult fracture); a clinically suspected scaphoid injury should be immobilised and re-imaged, or evaluated earlier with MRI or CT
Dedicated scaphoid views, including a posteroanterior projection in ulnar deviation, improve fracture detection compared with standard wrist films
Undisplaced waist fractures are usually managed with cast immobilisation, whereas displaced, unstable or proximal pole fractures often require percutaneous or open fixation
Untreated non-union may progress to a predictable pattern of carpal collapse and arthritis (scaphoid non-union advanced collapse)
reference.pathophysiology: The scaphoid spans the proximal and distal carpal rows and derives most of its blood supply from vessels that enter the distal pole and dorsal ridge, perfusing the bone in a retrograde direction. A fracture, most often across the waist, can interrupt flow to the proximal fragment, which becomes prone to delayed union, non-union and avascular necrosis. Because the bone is largely covered by articular cartilage with little periosteum, healing depends heavily on this tenuous vascular supply and on adequate immobilisation or fixation to prevent motion at the fracture. Persistent non-union alters carpal kinematics and leads over time to progressive degenerative collapse of the wrist.
additionalDifferentials: Fracture of the trapezium or other carpal bones
additionalInvestigations: Dedicated scaphoid radiographic series including a posteroanterior view in ulnar deviation, oblique and lateral projections
Repeat radiographs after an interval of immobilisation when initial films are normal but clinical suspicion persists
MRI for early detection of an occult fracture and marrow oedema
CT to characterise fracture displacement, humpback deformity and to assess union
Radionuclide bone scan as an alternative when MRI is unavailable
redFlags: Proximal pole fracture carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union
Fracture displacement or humpback (flexion) deformity indicating instability
Delayed presentation with established non-union or sclerosis
A snuffbox-tender wrist discharged on the basis of normal initial radiographs
reference.prognosis: Undisplaced waist fractures usually unite with adequate immobilisation, but proximal pole and displaced fractures carry substantially higher rates of non-union and avascular necrosis; unaddressed non-union can culminate in carpal collapse and post-traumatic arthritis.
pitfalls: Discharging a clinically suspicious, snuffbox-tender wrist because early radiographs appear normal
Underestimating the vascular vulnerability of proximal pole fractures
Inadequate duration or quality of immobilisation leading to non-union
Overlooking associated carpal ligament injury or instability
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Immobilise undisplaced waist fractures in a cast until radiographic union, given the tenuous retrograde blood supply
Refer displaced, unstable, or proximal pole fractures for percutaneous or open screw fixation
Immobilise clinically suspected but radiographically occult fractures and re-image, or arrange early MRI, rather than discharging
Provide analgesia and, after immobilisation, hand therapy to restore wrist and grip function
Confirm union with CT and monitor for non-union and avascular necrosis, particularly in proximal fractures
Refer to a hand or orthopaedic surgeon for displaced injuries and for suspected non-union or avascular necrosis
